## Keep the happy path in global handlers, and put edge cases in the test that needs them

_medium · typescript, msw_

**Rule.** Put the happy path in the shared handlers, and override an error or edge case inside its test with
`server.use()`. Call `server.resetHandlers()` after each test.

**Why.** Edge cases in the shared handlers separate a test from the response it depends on, and an override with no
reset leaks into the next test, which then fails or passes for the wrong reason.

**Incorrect:**

```tsx
// handlers.ts: a magic id selects the failure a test in another file wants
http.get("/api/invoices/:id", ({ params }) =>
  params.id === "broken" ? new HttpResponse(null, { status: 500 }) : HttpResponse.json(invoice),
);
```

**Correct:**

```tsx
test("shows an error when the invoice fails to load", async () => {
  server.use(http.get("/api/invoices/:id", () => new HttpResponse(null, { status: 500 })));
  render(<InvoicePage id="1" />);
  expect(await screen.findByRole("alert")).toHaveTextContent(/could not load/i);
});
```

## Assert what the user sees or can do, never internal state or markup

_medium · any_

**Rule.** Assert on what a user or assistive technology perceives: visible text, values, enabled or disabled
state, focus, ARIA attributes, and the calls a callback received. Leave internal state, class names
that carry no meaning for the user, and markup snapshots out of assertions.

**Why.** Tests that read internals break on every refactor that changes nothing for the user, and still pass
when the user-facing behaviour is broken, so the suite stops being trusted.

## Keep test setup inline until repetition hides what differs between tests

_medium · any_

**Rule.** Write a test's data and setup inline first. Extract a helper once repetition hides what differs between
tests; it takes overrides and returns what the test needs, with no branch per case, so a reader sees the
difference between two similar tests at once.

**Why.** A shared helper with an `if` for every case makes the reader step through it to learn what one test does,
and copied setups bury the one line that differs.

## Derive the expected value from the test's own input, not a repeated literal

_medium · any_

**Rule.** When the expected value follows from the test's input, compute it from that input: the row count
from the list the test rendered, a field's value from the value the test prefilled. Write a literal
only for a value the test introduces in the assertion itself.

**Why.** A hard-coded copy of the input goes stale the moment the input changes, so the test fails for a
reason unrelated to the code, or keeps passing against the wrong number.

## Keep snapshots small and inline, for output whose exact text matters

_medium · any_

**Rule.** Snapshot only small output whose exact text matters, such as error messages, logs or transformed code,
and keep the snapshot inline in the test. Replace a large snapshot with explicit assertions.

**Why.** A 600-line snapshot states no intent, so when it fails everyone overwrites it and moves on, and a real
regression goes in with the update.

## Query by the text users read, not by translation keys

_medium · any_

**Rule.** Query and assert on text as a user reads it in the default locale, never on the translation key behind it.

**Why.** A test that looks for `auth.username` still passes after the label changes from "Username" to "Email",
which is exactly the change a test should report.

## Use semantic HTML instead of adding ARIA so that a query works

_medium · any_

**Rule.** Use the semantic element and give inputs a `type`, so the implicit role is correct. Add `role` or
`aria-*` only for what HTML cannot express, and never just to make a test's query find an element.

**Why.** A `role="button"` on a `div` makes the query pass while the element still has no keyboard behaviour, so
the test reports an accessible control that users do not have. On a `button` the same attribute is noise.

## Choose the next test by what would hurt most if it broke

_medium · any_

**Rule.** Pick the next test by asking what in the untested part of the app would hurt most if it broke. Narrow
that to one or a few units of code, name who uses them, write the instructions you would give a manual
tester, and turn those instructions into the automated test.

**Why.** Tests chosen by walking through branches, loops and lifecycles cover code nobody would miss while the
checkout flow stays untested, so effort goes up and confidence does not.

## Judge a suite by the use cases it covers, not by a coverage percentage

_medium · any_

**Rule.** Use a coverage report only to find code without tests, and judge a suite by which use cases it covers.
Set no percentage target for an application, and do not measure coverage on E2E tests.

**Why.** A percentage target gets met with tests of the cheapest lines, so a suite can report 100% while an
unhandled use case ships broken.

**Exceptions.** A small open source library used in many places can justify aiming for 100%.

## Answer an act warning by waiting for the effect, not by wrapping calls in act

_medium · typescript, react, testing-library_

**Rule.** Call `render` and user-event without `act`, since they already wrap their work in it. When the warning
appears, wait for the visible effect with `findBy*`, `waitFor` or `waitForElementToBeRemoved`.

**Why.** The warning usually means something happens after the test completes, so wrapping a call silences it and
leaves that state update unchecked.

**Incorrect:**

```tsx
await act(async () => {
  render(<SaveButton />);
});
await user.click(screen.getByRole("button", { name: /save/i }));
```

**Correct:**

```tsx
render(<SaveButton />);
await user.click(screen.getByRole("button", { name: /save/i }));
await waitForElementToBeRemoved(() => screen.queryByText(/saving/i));
```

**Exceptions.** Call `act` directly for what happens outside the React call stack and outside Testing Library's utilities:
advancing fake timers, methods from `useImperativeHandle`, direct calls to a hook's functions, and async
work with no visible effect.

## Lint tests with the Testing Library and jest-dom ESLint plugins

_medium · typescript, react, testing-library_

**Rule.** Turn on `eslint-plugin-testing-library` with its React preset and `eslint-plugin-jest-dom` with its
recommended rules, for test files only.

**Why.** Without them, a misused query or a weak matcher reaches review or stays in the suite for good, even though
a linter can flag and often autofix it on save.

**Incorrect:**

```ts
// eslint.config.ts: test files get only the general rules
export default [...tseslint.configs.recommended];
```

**Correct:**

```ts
export default [
  ...tseslint.configs.recommended,
  { files: ["**/*.test.tsx"], ...testingLibrary.configs["flat/react"] },
  { files: ["**/*.test.tsx"], ...jestDom.configs["flat/recommended"] },
];
```

## Leave cleanup to the test setup, not to each test file

_medium · typescript, react, testing-library, vitest_

**Rule.** Write no `cleanup` call in a test file. Under a runner with a global `afterEach` it happens automatically;
under Vitest without `globals: true`, register it once in the setup file.

**Why.** A cleanup line copied into every file does nothing where cleanup is automatic, and where it is not, the
file that forgets it leaks a mounted tree into the next test.

**Incorrect:**

```tsx
// invoice-list.test.tsx
afterEach(cleanup);

test("lists invoices", () => {
  render(<InvoiceList invoices={invoices} />);
});
```

**Correct:**

```tsx
// vitest.setup.ts, only when globals is off
afterEach(() => {
  cleanup();
});
```

## Write one test per user flow, with all its steps and assertions

_medium · typescript, react, testing-library_

**Rule.** Cover one manual tester's flow in one test: one Arrange, then as many Act and Assert steps as the flow
needs. Render the component once per test, apart from `rerender` when a prop change is the point.

**Why.** Five one-assertion tests render the same component five times and split a flow so that no test proves it
works from start to finish. Test runners already show exactly which assertion failed.

**Incorrect:**

```tsx
test("shows a spinner", async () => {
  render(<Profile />);
  expect(screen.getByRole("progressbar")).toBeVisible();
});
test("shows the name", async () => {
  render(<Profile />);
  expect(await screen.findByRole("heading", { name: "Ann" })).toBeVisible();
});
```

**Correct:**

```tsx
test("loads and shows the profile", async () => {
  render(<Profile />);
  expect(screen.getByRole("progressbar")).toBeVisible();
  expect(await screen.findByRole("heading", { name: "Ann" })).toBeVisible();
  expect(screen.queryByRole("progressbar")).not.toBeInTheDocument();
});
```

## Drive interactions with user-event, not fireEvent

_medium · typescript, react, testing-library_

**Rule.** Drive every interaction with `@testing-library/user-event`, creating the instance with
`userEvent.setup()` before `render` and awaiting each call.

**Why.** `fireEvent` dispatches a single event, so a handler on `keydown` goes unexercised and a test can type into
a field a real user could not reach.

**Incorrect:**

```tsx
render(<SignupForm />);
fireEvent.change(screen.getByLabelText(/email/i), { target: { value: "a@b.co" } });
```

**Correct:**

```tsx
const user = userEvent.setup();
render(<SignupForm />);
await user.type(screen.getByLabelText(/email/i), "a@b.co");
```

## Query through screen, not through what render returns

_medium · typescript, react, testing-library_

**Rule.** Query through `screen`, and debug with `screen.debug()`. Destructure from `render` only what `screen` does
not give, such as `rerender`, and never keep its result in a variable called `wrapper`.

**Why.** Queries destructured from `render` have to be threaded through every helper and go stale in long tests,
so test files fill up with plumbing that `screen` makes unnecessary.

**Incorrect:**

```tsx
const { getByRole } = render(<SignupForm />);
expect(getByRole("button", { name: /sign up/i })).toBeEnabled();
```

**Correct:**

```tsx
render(<SignupForm />);
expect(screen.getByRole("button", { name: /sign up/i })).toBeEnabled();
```

## Share component test setup through a helper, not nested describe and beforeEach

_medium · typescript, react, testing-library_

**Rule.** Keep a component test file flat, with data and setup inline or from a `setup()` function that returns what
the test needs. Group tests by file, and use `before*` and `after*` only for cleanup and global resources
such as the MSW server.

**Why.** Variables assigned in hooks make the reader trace values through the whole file to learn what one test
does, and an override in a nested block changes tests it does not seem to touch.

**Incorrect:**

```tsx
let user: UserEvent;
beforeEach(() => {
  user = userEvent.setup();
  render(<LoginForm onSubmit={onSubmit} />);
});
describe("when submitted", () => {
  test("calls onSubmit", async () => { /* … */ });
});
```

**Correct:**

```tsx
function setup() {
  const onSubmit = vi.fn();
  render(<LoginForm onSubmit={onSubmit} />);
  return { user: userEvent.setup(), onSubmit };
}

test("calls onSubmit when submitted", async () => {
  const { user, onSubmit } = setup();
  /* … */
});
```

## Test a custom hook through a component that uses it before reaching for renderHook

_medium · typescript, react, testing-library_

**Rule.** Cover a hook used by one component through that component's tests, and a reusable hook through a small
example component. Use `renderHook` when that component would be too complex or the cases too many, and
never mock `useState` or `useEffect` to call a hook as a plain function.

**Why.** A hook tested alone, or with React's own hooks mocked, passes while the component that uses it is broken,
because nothing has run it the way the app does.

**Incorrect:**

```tsx
vi.spyOn(React, "useState").mockReturnValue([0, setCount]);
useCounter().increment();
expect(setCount).toHaveBeenCalledWith(1);
```

**Correct:**

```tsx
function Example() {
  const { count, increment } = useCounter();
  return <button onClick={increment}>{count}</button>;
}

render(<Example />);
await user.click(screen.getByRole("button", { name: "0" }));
expect(screen.getByRole("button", { name: "1" })).toBeInTheDocument();
```

## Write the test first when the requirements are clear

_low · any_

**Rule.** Write the test first when the requirements are clear: pure functions, bug fixes, UIs with a well-defined
design. In exploratory coding, add the tests once the direction has settled.

**Why.** Tests written first during exploration get rewritten with every change of direction, and tests postponed
on clear requirements give up the fastest feedback available.
